extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Euclidean solid geometry (students, teachers, mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Euclid's Elements, Book XI: statements and proofs of propositions about planes, perpendiculars, parallelism, solid angles, and solids (solid geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of perpendicular from a point to a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: From a point above a plane there can be but one perpendicular to that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if two perpendiculars from the same point existed they would be parallel, which is impossible; uses fact that a line perpendicular to a plane makes right angles with every line in the plane meeting it. (Q.E.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Planes to which the same straight line is perpendicular are parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: Planes to which the same straight line is perpendicular are parallel to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let a line be perpendicular to two planes. If the planes met, pick a point on their intersection and form triangle with the given line; then two angles would be right angles producing contradiction (two angles of a triangle equal to two right angles). Therefore the planes do not meet and are parallel. (Proposition XIV)

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelism of planes through corresponding parallel line-pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: If two straight lines meeting one another are parallel to two straight lines which meet one another but are not in the same plane with the first two, the plane which passes through the first two is parallel to the plane passing through the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a line from the intersection point perpendicular to the plane of the second pair; construct parallels to the given lines through that foot to show the perpendicular stands at right angles to both planes, then apply the previous proposition that planes to which the same line is perpendicular are parallel. (Proposition XV)

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersections of parallel planes with a third plane are parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: If two parallel planes be cut by another plane, their common sections with it are parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume intersection lines meet and derive that their intersection point would lie in both parallel planes, contradicting their non-meeting. Hence intersection lines do not meet and are parallel. (Proposition XVI)

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel planes cut parallel lines in the same ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: If two straight lines be cut by parallel planes, they shall be cut in the same ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given two lines cut by a sequence of parallel planes, join corresponding endpoints to form triangles, use parallels to show corresponding segments are proportional, and combine equalities to conclude AE:EB = CF:FD. (Proposition XVII)

rubrics_metrics.name: Planes through a line perpendicular to a plane are perpendicular to that plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line be at right angles to a plane, every plane which passes through that straight line shall be at right angles to the plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take any plane through the given perpendicular line, consider its common section with the given plane, pick a point on that section and construct a perpendicular in the chosen plane; because the given line is perpendicular to the given plane it is perpendicular to that common section, leading to perpendicularity of the constructed line and hence of the plane. (Proposition XVIII)

rubrics_metrics.name: Common section of two planes each perpendicular to a third is perpendicular
rubrics_metrics.description: If two planes cutting one another be each of them perpendicular to a third plane, their common section shall be perpendicular to the same plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the common section is not perpendicular; construct two different perpendiculars from the intersection point to the third plane lying on the two planes, yielding two distinct perpendiculars from the same point to the same plane, contradicting uniqueness. (Proposition XIX)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two of the three plane angles of a solid angle exceed the third
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid angle be contained by three plane angles, any two of them are greater than the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare plane angles by constructing equal angles and equal segments; use triangle inequalities (sides/bases comparisons lead to angle comparisons) to show sum of any two plane angles exceeds the third. (Proposition XX)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of plane angles of a solid angle is less than four right angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Every solid angle is contained by plane angles which together are less than four right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split into triangles by taking points on the rays and summing angles at those points; use facts about plane polygons and triangles (sum of polygon angles with four right angles) to bound the sum of the vertex plane angles by less than four right angles. (Proposition XXI)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructibility condition for triangle from three equal-length rays with angle-sum conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If every two of three plane angles be greater than the third, and if the straight lines which contain them be all equal, then a triangle may be made of the straight lines that join the extremities of those equal straight lines (i.e., the three joining segments satisfy triangle inequalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cases where corresponding angles are equal or not; using angle and side comparisons (and constructing auxiliary equal segments and angles) show any two of the joining segments are greater than the third, hence they form a triangle. (Proposition XXII)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a solid angle from three given plane angles
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a solid angle which shall be contained by three given plane angles, any two of them being greater than the third, and all three together less than four right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut off equal segments on lines containing the given angles, join them to make a triangle, circumscribe a circle, take its centre X and distinguish cases according to X's location; erect a perpendicular at X to the plane and construct a tripod of equal lines from the perpendicular to the triangle's vertices to produce three planes with prescribed plane angles equal to the given ones. The proof examines multiple positions of the circle center and resolves contradictions to ensure existence of desired solid angle. (Proposition XXIII / Problem)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of inclinations of corresponding planes in equal solid angles
rubrics_metrics.description: If each of two solid angles be contained by three plane angles equal to one another, each to each, then the planes in which the equal angles are have the same inclination to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take equal segments on corresponding rays and build right-angled lines to the rays in the respective planes; show pairs of corresponding perpendicular segments are equal and hence the angle between those perpendiculars (the inclination) is equal. (Proposition A)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of solid angles with corresponding equal plane angles similarly situated
rubrics_metrics.description: If two solid angles be contained, each by three plane angles which are equal to one another, each to each, and alike situated, then these solid angles are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the solid angle at one point to the other matching corresponding plane angles and using equal inclinations to make the planes coincide; thus the solids coincide and are equal. (Proposition B)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality and similarity of solid figures with equal/similar faces
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid figures contained by the same number of equal and similar planes alike situated, and having none of their solid angles contained by more than three plane angles, are equal and similar to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match corresponding faces and solid angles and apply successive plane-by-plane coincidences (using previous propositions about solid angles and plane inclinations) to show full coincidence of solids; hence equality and similarity follow. (Proposition C)

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposite faces of a six-faced solid with two-by-two parallel faces are equal and similar parallelograms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid be contained by six planes, two and two of which are parallel, the opposite planes are similar and equal parallelograms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut the solid by planes and use intersections to show opposite faces are parallelograms; compare triangles formed by corresponding intersections to show opposite parallelograms are equal and similar pairwise. (Proposition XXIV)

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane parallel to opposite faces divides parallelepiped proportionally
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solid parallelepiped be cut by a plane parallel to two of its opposite planes, it divides the whole into two solids, the base of one of which shall be to the base of the other as the one solid is to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend edges to form multiple equal parallelograms and solids, decompose the parallelepiped into repeated equal solids and compare multiples to deduce the proportionality between bases and volumes of the two resulting solids. (Proposition XXV)
